text: From the meta-learning perspective, the dynamic selection problem can be seen as another classification problem, called the meta-problem. This meta-problem uses different criteria regarding the behavior of a base classifier in order to decide whether it is competent enough to classify a given sample 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j}. Thus, a dynamic selection system can be defined based on two environments. A classification environment in which the input features are mapped into a set of class labels w={w1,w2,…,wL}w=\left\{w_{1},w_{2},...,w_{L}\right\} and a meta-classification environment in which information about the behavior of the base classifier is extracted from the classification environment and used to decide whether a base classifier cic_{i} is competent enough to classify 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j}.
To keep with the conventions of the meta-learning literature, we define the proposed dynamic ensemble selection in a meta-learning framework as follows:
The meta-problem consists in defining whether a base classifier cic_{i} is competent enough to classify 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j}.
The meta-classes of this meta-problem are either “competent” or “incompetent” to classify 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j}.
Each meta-feature fif_{i} corresponds to a different criterion to measure the level of competence of a base classifier.

The meta-features are encoded into a meta-features vector vi,jv_{i,j} which contains the information about the behavior of a base classifier cic_{i} in relation to the input instance 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j}.
A meta-classifier λ\lambda is trained based on the meta-features vi,jv_{i,j} to predict whether or not cic_{i} will achieve the correct prediction for 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j}.

In other words, a meta-classifier λ\lambda is trained, based on vi,jv_{i,j}, to predict whether a base classifier cic_{i} is competent enough to classify given a test sample 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j}. Thus, the proposed system differs from the current state-of-the-art dynamic selection techniques not only because it uses multiple criteria, but also because the selection rule is learned by the meta-classifier λ\lambda using the training data.
The META-DES framework is divided into three phases (Figure 1):

The overproduction phase, where the pool of classifiers C={c1,…,cM}C=\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{M}\}, composed of MM classifiers, is generated using the training instances 𝐱j,t​r​a​i​n\mathbf{x}_{j,train} from the dataset 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

The meta-training stage, in which samples 𝐱j,t​r​a​i​nλ\mathbf{x}_{j,train_{\lambda}} from the meta-training dataset 𝒯λ\mathcal{T}_{\lambda} are used to extract the meta-features. A different dataset 𝒯λ\mathcal{T}_{\lambda} is used in this phase in order to prevent overfitting. The meta-feature vectors vi,jv_{i,j} are stored in the set 𝒯λ∗\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}^{*} that is later used to train the meta-classifier λ\lambda.

The generalization phase, given a test sample 𝐱j,t​e​s​t\mathbf{x}_{j,test} resulting from the generalization data 𝒢\mathcal{G}; its region of competence is extracted using the samples from the dynamic selection dataset DS​E​LD_{SEL} in order to compute the meta-features. The meta-feature vector vi,jv_{i,j} is then passed to the selector λ\lambda, which decides whether cic_{i} is competent enough to classify 𝐱j,t​e​s​t\mathbf{x}_{j,test} and should be added to the ensemble, C′C^{\prime}. The majority vote rule is applied over the ensemble C′C^{\prime}, giving the classification wlw_{l} of 𝐱j,t​e​s​t\mathbf{x}_{j,test}.

In this work, the Overproduction phase is performed using the Bagging technique [32, 33]. Bagging is an acronym for Bootstrap AGGregatING. The idea behind this technique is to build a diverse ensemble of classifiers by randomly selecting different subsets of the training data. Each subset is used to train one individual classifier cic_{i}. As the focus of the paper is on classifier selection, and not on classifier generation methods, only the bagging technique is considered.

As shown in Figure 1, the meta-training stage consists of three steps: the sample selection process, the meta-features extraction process, and the training of the meta-classifier λ\lambda. For every sample 𝐱j,t​r​a​i​nλ∈𝒯λ\mathbf{x}_{j,train_{\lambda}}\in\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}, the first step is to apply the sample selection mechanism in order to know whether or not 𝐱j,t​r​a​i​nλ\mathbf{x}_{j,train_{\lambda}} should be used for the training of the meta-classifier λ\lambda. The whole Meta-training phase is formalized in Algorithm 1.

As demonstrated by Dos Santos et al. [5] and Cavalin et al. [6], one of the main issues in dynamic ensemble selection arises when classifying testing instances where the degree of consensus among the pool of classifier is low, i.e., when the number of votes from the winning class is close or even equal to the number of votes from the second class. To tackle this issue, we decided to focus the training of the meta-classifier λ\lambda to specifically deal with cases where the extent of consensus among the pool is low. This step is conducted using a threshold hCh_{C}, called the consensus threshold. Each instance 𝐱j,t​r​a​i​nλ\mathbf{x}_{j,train_{\lambda}} is first evaluated by the whole pool of classifiers in order to compute the degree of consensus among the pool, denoted by H⁡(𝐱j,t​r​a​i​nλ,C)H\left(\mathbf{x}_{j,train_{\lambda}},C\right). If the consensus H⁡(𝐱j,t​r​a​i​nλ,C)H\left(\mathbf{x}_{j,train_{\lambda}},C\right) falls below the consensus threshold hCh_{C}, the instance 𝐱j,t​r​a​i​nλ\mathbf{x}_{j,train_{\lambda}} is used to compute the meta-features.

Before extracting the meta-features, the region of competence of the instance 𝐱j,t​r​a​i​nλ\mathbf{x}_{j,train_{\lambda}}, denoted by θj={𝐱1,…,𝐱K}\theta_{j}=\left\{\mathbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{K}\right\}, must first be computed. The region of competence θj\theta_{j} is defined in the 𝒯λ\mathcal{T_{\lambda}} set, using the K-Nearest Neighbor algorithm (line 5). Then, 𝐱j,t​r​a​i​nλ\mathbf{x}_{j,train_{\lambda}} is transformed into an output profile. The output profile of the instance 𝐱j,t​r​a​i​nλ\mathbf{x}_{j,train_{\lambda}} is denoted by 𝐱~j,t​r​a​i​nλ={𝐱~j,t​r​a​i​nλ,1,𝐱~j,t​r​a​i​nλ,2,…,𝐱~j,t​r​a​i​nλ,M}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{j,train_{\lambda}}=\left\{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{j,train_{\lambda},1},\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{j,train_{\lambda},2},\ldots,\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{j,train_{\lambda},M}\right\}, where each 𝐱~j,t​r​a​i​nλ,i\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{j,train_{\lambda},i} is the decision yielded by the base classifier cic_{i} for the sample 𝐱j,t​r​a​i​nλ\mathbf{x}_{j,train_{\lambda}} [6, 7].

Next, with the region of competence θj\theta_{j} and the set with the most similar output profiles ϕj\phi_{j} computed, for each base classifier cic_{i} belonging to the pool of classifiers CC, one meta-feature vector vi,jv_{i,j} is extracted (lines 8 to 14). Each vi,jv_{i,j} contains five sets of meta-features:

Five different sets of meta-features are proposed in this work. Each feature set fif_{i}, corresponds to a different criterion for measuring the level of competence of a base classifier. Each set captures a different property about the behavior of the base classifier, and can be seen as a different criterion to dynamically estimate the level of competence of base classifier such as, the classification performance estimated in a local region of the feature space and the classifier confidence for the classification of the input sample. Using five distinct sets of meta-features, even though one criterion might fail due to imprecisions in the local regions of the feature space or due to low confidence results, the system can still achieve a good performance as other meta-features are considered by the selection scheme. Table 1 shows the criterion used by each fif_{i} and its relationship with one dynamic ensemble selection paradigm presented in Section 2.

Three meta-features, f1f_{1}, f2f_{2} and f3f_{3}, are computed using information extracted from the region of competence θj\theta_{j}. f4f_{4} uses information extracted from the set of output profiles ϕj\phi_{j}. f5f_{5} is calculated directly from the input sample 𝐱j,t​r​a​i​nλ\mathbf{x}_{j,train_{\lambda}}, and corresponds to the level of confidence of cic_{i} for the classification of 𝐱j,t​r​a​i​nλ\mathbf{x}_{j,train_{\lambda}}.

First, a vector with KK elements is created. For each instance 𝐱k\mathbf{x}_{k}, belonging to the region of competence θj\theta_{j}, if cic_{i} correctly classifies 𝐱k\mathbf{x}_{k}, the kk-th position of the vector is set to 1, otherwise it is 0. Thus, KK meta-features are computed.

First, a vector with KK elements is created. Then, for each instance 𝐱k\mathbf{x}_{k}, belonging to the region of competence θj\theta_{j}, the posterior probability of cic_{i}, P⁡(wl∣𝐱k)P(w_{l}\mid\mathbf{x}_{k}) is computed and inserted into the kk-th position of the vector. Consequently, KK meta-features are computed.
The accuracy of cic_{i} over the whole region of competence θj\theta_{j} is computed and encoded as f3f_{3}.

First, a vector with KpK_{p} elements is generated. Then, for each member 𝐱~k\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{k} belonging to the set of output profiles ϕj\phi_{j}, if the label produced by cic_{i} for 𝐱k\mathbf{x}_{k} is equal to the label wl,kw_{l,k} of 𝐱~k\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{k}, the kk-th position of the vector is set to 1, otherwise it is 0. A total of KpK_{p} meta-features are extracted using output profiles.

The perpendicular distance between the input sample 𝐱j,t​r​a​i​nλ\mathbf{x}_{j,train_{\lambda}} and the decision boundary of the base classifier cic_{i} is calculated and encoded as f5f_{5}. f5f_{5} is normalized to a [0−1][0-1] range using the Min-max normalization.

A vector vi,j={f1∪f2∪f3∪f4∪f5}v_{i,j}=\left\{f_{1}\cup f_{2}\cup f_{3}\cup f_{4}\cup f_{5}\right\} is obtained at the end of the process (Figure 2). If cic_{i} correctly classifies 𝐱j,t​r​a​i​nλ\mathbf{x}_{j,train_{\lambda}}, the class attribute of vi,jv_{i,j}, αi,j=1\alpha_{i,j}=1 (i.e., vi,jv_{i,j} corresponds to the behavior of a competent classifier), otherwise αi,j=0\alpha_{i,j}=0. vi,jv_{i,j} is stored in the meta-features dataset 𝒯λ∗\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}^{*} (lines 10 to 16).

For each sample 𝐱j,t​r​a​i​nλ\mathbf{x}_{j,train_{\lambda}} used in the meta-training stage, a total of MM (MM is the size of the pool of classifiers CC) meta-feature vectors vi,jv_{i,j} are extracted, each one corresponding to one classifier from the pool CC. In this way, the size of the meta-training dataset 𝒯λ∗\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}^{*} is the pool size M×M\times number of training samples NN. For instance, consider that 200200 training samples are available for the meta-training stage (N=200N=200), if the pool CC is composed of 100100 weak classifiers (M=100M=100), the meta-training dataset is the number of training samples NN ×\times the number classifiers in the pool MM, N∗M=20.000N*M=20.000. Hence, even though the classification problem may be ill-defined due to the size of the training set, we can overcome this limitation in the meta-problem by increasing the size of the pool of classifiers.

The last step of the meta-training phase is the training of the meta-classifier λ\lambda. The dataset 𝒯λ∗\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}^{*} is divided on the basis of 75% for training and 25% for validation. A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) neural network is considered as the selector λ\lambda. The validation data was used to select the number of nodes in the hidden layer. We use a configuration of 10 neurons in the hidden layer since there were no improvement in results with more than 10 neurons. The training process for λ\lambda is performed using the Levenberg-Marquadt algorithm. In addition, the training process is stopped if its performance on the validation set decreases or fails to improve for five consecutive epochs.

The generalization procedure is formalized by Algorithm 2. Given the query sample 𝐱j,t​e​s​t\mathbf{x}_{j,test}, in this phase, the region of competence θj\theta_{j} is computed using the samples from the dynamic selection dataset DS​E​LD_{SEL} (line 2). Following that, the output profiles 𝐱~j,t​e​s​t\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{j,test} of the test sample, 𝐱j,t​e​s​t\mathbf{x}_{j,test}, are calculated. The set with KpK_{p} similar output profiles ϕj\phi_{j}, of the query sample 𝐱j,t​e​s​t\mathbf{x}_{j,test}, is obtained through the Euclidean distance applied over the output profiles of the dynamic selection dataset, D~S​E​L\tilde{D}_{SEL}.

Next, for each classifier cic_{i} belonging to the pool of classifiers CC, the meta-feature extraction process is called (Section 3.2.2.2), returning the meta-features vector vi,jv_{i,j} (lines 5 and 6). Then, vi,jv_{i,j} is used as input to the meta-classifier λ\lambda. If the output of λ\lambda is 11 (i.e., competent), cic_{i} is included in the ensemble C′C^{\prime} (lines 8 to 10). After every base classifier, cic_{i}, is evaluated, the ensemble C′C^{\prime} is obtained. The base classifiers in C′C^{\prime} are combined through the Majority Vote rule [1], giving the label wlw_{l} of xj,t​e​s​tx_{j,test} (line 12 and 13). The majority vote rule is used to combine the selected classifiers since it has been successfully used by other DES techniques [3]. Tie-breaking is handled by choosing the class with the highest a posteriori probability.
